metadata.title: Downfall: First Blender Assets for the Terraces
metadata.note: godot-gamedev, walker mode, Assignment 3. Engine media are native 3840x2160 Godot Movie Maker captures from an isolated clone of ceada15 (window override + MJPEG quality only); Blender views are Claude's MCP look images; B17 is the author's own screenshot. See CAPTURE.md.

beats.narration_text: Hola. Liam, in for Bear. This is a reconstructed ask, not a transcript. A student wanted Walker to take the design for Downfall's new terraced field maps and turn it into the game's first three Blender assets, built through Blender MCP and checked inside Godot.

props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about Downfall's terraced field maps into three Blender assets: a cliff wall segment, an arched ramp segment and a cliff rubble pile, built through Blender MCP and checked in Godot.
output: Reconstructed prompt - illustrative, not a transcript.

beats.narration_text: Here's the honest version. Claude built all three assets by sending Python to Blender through MCP, one call per part, and every call is kept in the repo. The author made the design calls, learned the viewport, moved two kerbs by hand, and gave the final look. One difference up front: this was Blender five point four alpha, not the course's five point one.

show.event: 'Built in the course Blender' types and pauses

props.text:

beats.narration_text: The assignment: three game assets, each in its own Blender file. At most six primitives and under five hundred triangles each, flat colours only, no sculpting, textures, rigging or animation, modelled around the origin with the bottom on the ground. Downfall's field maps had just become terraces, so these three dress them: a cliff wall, a ramp, and the rubble at a cliff's foot.

beats.narration_text: Every size starts in the game's map generator. A terrace level is two point two metres. A ramp needs at least six point five metres of run per level, which is under nineteen degrees, plus two flat metres at each end. And a corridor's half-width is rolled between three point four and five point six, so the narrowest corridor is six point eight wide.

beats.narration_text: Here is that in the running game. On the mine floor with map seed seventeen twenty-nine, she stands at a ramp's foot. On seed thirteen thirty-three, she stands below a cliff between two terraces. The terrain mesh already gives every ramp and cliff its shape and its collision, which is how Grim Dawn's editor works too. So these assets are dressing, laid on top.

beats.narration_text: The cliff segment is three stacked boxes and one icosphere: one terrace tall, plus a tenth of a metre above and below, and only point three in front of the face. This is the sixth call. After the first look, the boulder on top was mostly buried and read as a flat disc. This call makes it half a metre tall and moves it onto the front lip, still peaking at two point four.

show.event: Godot editor reconstruction: tools/blender/build_cliff_wall_segment.py lines 95-107, revision ceada15

props.title: A fix after looking
props.code:
# --- call 6 ---
# Step 4b (fix after look): the boulder was buried 0.2 of its 0.35 in strata_top and read as a disc.
# Make it 0.8 x 0.6 x 0.5 and set it on the front lip so it bulges out of the face:
# z 1.9-2.4 (peak still 2.4), front at y = -0.30 (the brief's front limit).
import bpy
obj = bpy.data.objects["lip_boulder"]
d = obj.dimensions.copy()
obj.scale = (0.80 / d.x, 0.60 / d.y, 0.50 / d.z)
bpy.ops.object.select_all(action="DESELECT")
obj.select_set(True)
bpy.context.view_layer.objects.active = obj
bpy.ops.object.transform_apply(location=False, rotation=True, scale=True)
obj.location = (0.75, 0.0, 2.40 - 0.25)

notes.label: Before
notes.value: 0.35 tall, centred on the top stratum: 0.2 buried

beats.narration_text: Claude's look views, before and after: front, right, top, and three-quarter. Before, a thin disc on the top stratum. After, the boulder bulges out of the face. The rubble pile had the same kind of miss. Its top stone floated, and the next call sank it into the stone below.

beats.narration_text: The ramp is one plane, edited into a solid wedge, plus two kerbs. Its top follows this function: the slope, two point two over six point five, plus two centimetres so it never fights the terrain, plus a ten-centimetre crown on the centre line. The crown fades to nothing over the first and last half metre, so neither end has a lip.

show.event: Godot editor reconstruction: tools/blender/build_arched_ramp_segment.py lines 47-51, revision ceada15

props.title: The crown is one function
props.code:
RISE, RUN, HALF_W, CROWN, TAPER, CLEAR = 2.2, 6.5, 3.4, 0.10, 0.5, 0.02

def top_z(x, y):
    taper = max(0.0, min(1.0, min(y, RUN - y) / TAPER))
    return RISE * y / RUN + CLEAR + CROWN * (1.0 - abs(x) / HALF_W) * taper

beats.narration_text: The result: an edge slope of eighteen point seven degrees, and a crown of exactly point one, half a metre in. One honest observation: in Blender's solid shading the crown is barely visible, and from the game's camera it isn't visible at all.

beats.narration_text: One change was made by hand. The author opened the ramp in Blender and moved each kerb a tenth of a metre outward. The reason: the corridor's rock bank starts at three point four, so a kerb that ends exactly there leaves a seam. This comment records the steps Claude gave. The author's own report was just: all done.

# then saved (Ctrl+S). Overall width 6.8 -> 7.0. Reason: bury the kerb's outer edge

beats.narration_text: Claude then read the file back without changing it. The left kerb now spans minus three point five to minus three point two, the road is unchanged, and the right kerb mirrors it. The overall width is seven metres. The file was saved, and Blender wrote a backup file, which git now ignores.

shot.label: Recorded MCP output · get_scene_info and a read-only check

beats.narration_text: Export is headless: one script run per file, glTF binary, Y up, the mesh only. Blender's plus Y becomes Godot's minus Z. So the ramp should climb away from its origin towards minus Z, and the cliff's face should look towards plus Z.

show.event: Godot editor reconstruction: tools/blender/export_glb.py lines 24-33, revision ceada15

props.title: Blender +Y becomes Godot −Z
props.source: Godot editor reconstruction · tools/blender/export_glb.py:24-33 · commit ceada15
props.code:
bpy.ops.export_scene.gltf(
    filepath=out,
    export_format="GLB",
    use_selection=True,
    export_yup=True,
    export_apply=True,
    export_cameras=False,
    export_lights=False,
    export_materials="EXPORT",
)

beats.narration_text: And in Godot: a moment through the game's own camera, then one full orbit, front, side and behind. The blue capsule is one point seven metres, for scale. Note that the game camera looks from minus Z, so by default the cliff's face points away from it. Placing cliffs on the map will need a rotation per cliff line.

beats.narration_text: The headless check reads the imported meshes back. This part finds the ramp's highest vertices and requires them past minus six on Z. Other checks compare each bounding box with the brief to two centimetres, plus every node's transform, the triangle counts and the colours.

# F1: the high end must be at -Z. F4: the edge slope must stay under 19 deg.
		var high_z := 0.0
		var top_y := -1.0
		for p in points:
			if p.y > top_y - 0.001:
				if p.y > top_y + 0.001: high_z = p.z
				top_y = maxf(top_y, p.y)
		check("ramp: highest vertices at z %.2f (high end towards -Z)" % high_z, high_z < -6.0)

beats.narration_text: On a fresh copy of the commit, all twenty-five checks pass. That proves Blender, the glTF file and Godot agree. It does not prove the assets look right, or that they fit the generated terrain. Nor does it prove the normals face out: the exporter marked the materials double-sided, so Godot never hides a back face.

shot.label: Recorded test output · fresh copy of ceada15

beats.narration_text: One bug was in Claude's preview scene, not in the assets. In a Godot scene file, a transform's basis is written row by row. Claude wrote the sun's basis column by column. This is the corrected line.

show.event: Godot editor reconstruction: art/models/asset_preview.tscn lines 33-35, revision ceada15

props.title: Rows, not columns
props.source: Godot editor reconstruction · art/models/asset_preview.tscn:33-35 · commit ceada15
props.code:
[node name="Sun" type="DirectionalLight3D" parent="."]
transform = Transform3D(0.866025, 0, 0.5, -0.353553, -0.707107, 0.612372, 0.353553, -0.707107, -0.612372, 0, 10, 0)
shadow_enabled = true

beats.narration_text: Re-rendered with the basis as first written, the light points up. The stone tops go black and their sides glow, and it looks like flipped normals. Claude counted inward faces in Blender first, found none, and then found the transpose. With the corrected line, the tops catch the light and the shadows fall on the ground.

beats.narration_text: Verdict. Working: three assets at a hundred and sixteen, sixty-eight and a hundred and eighty triangles, sized from the game's own numbers, with twenty-five checks passing. Found and fixed: a buried boulder, a floating stone, Godot trying to import the Blender files, and an upside-down sun. Still open: none of this is placed on a real map yet, the cliff faces away from the game camera, and the human check was one line.

artifactLines: Working: cliff 116 · ramp 68 · rubble 180 triangles; sized from TIER, RAMP_RUN, half-width; 25/25 checks.
Fixed: buried boulder · floating stone · .blend auto-import (.gdignore) · sun basis rows vs columns.
Open: not placed by the map generator · cliff face points away from the game camera · ramp crown unreadable.
Human: author's kerb edit verified; human check reported in one line, recorded as given.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Before you run it, write down which check you expect to fail. Liam, in for Bear.
